In the academic discussion task you have about ten minutes, and I want you to divide them into three parts before you even read the question. The first minute is for the outline. Read the professor’s question and the two student posts, decide your position, and write down two reasons and one example, in single words, not sentences. The next eight minutes are for the draft. Do not repeat what the other students said; respond to one of them, and then add something new. And the last minute is sacred: you proofread. Look for the mistakes you always make, not every possible mistake. Most students skip the outline because it feels like wasted time. It is the opposite. The outline is what keeps your answer coherent when the clock starts to feel loud.

I always ask students to plan backwards. Start with the deadline and ask where you will be one week before it. By then, you will have sent your documents, and you will be waiting for an answer. Two months before that, you will have received your official score. And for that to happen, you will be taking the test about four months before the deadline, so that there is still time to retake it. Now go back further. A year before the deadline, you will be writing under real time limits every week, and by that point you will have taken at least one full practice test. When you see it like this, two years is not a long time. It is a timeline with five or six milestones, and the most important one is the first practice test, because it tells you how far you really are from the requirement.
